lead: A real band-pass signal carries information in a narrow band around a carrier, so the carrier is only a vehicle. The Hilbert transform turns the real signal into an analytic signal that has only positive frequencies. Removing the carrier from that analytic signal leaves the complex envelope, a low-pass complex signal whose real and imaginary parts are the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. This idea is used in SSB generation, I/Q modulators, digital receivers and simulation of band-pass systems.
prereq: You need the Fourier transform and band-pass spectra from 1.2; modulation basics are in 1.1.

blocks.text: Real signals have a conjugate-symmetric spectrum, X(−f) = X*(f), so the negative-frequency half carries no new information and the positive half alone can describe the signal. The Hilbert transform produces a companion signal x̂(t) that is 90° shifted in phase without changing the magnitude spectrum.

blocks.where: x̂(t) is the Hilbert transform of x(t) in volts; PV means the Cauchy principal value, which avoids the singular point τ = t; τ is the integration variable in seconds.
H(f) is the frequency response; sgn(f) = 1 for f > 0, −1 for f < 0 and 0 at f = 0; f is frequency in hertz; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: For positive frequencies, H(f) = −j gives a −90° phase shift. For negative frequencies it gives +90°. At f = 0 the response is zero. The transform is all-pass: every frequency keeps its amplitude.

items: H[cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + θ)] = sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + θ) for f<sub>c</sub> > 0. Cos becomes sin, not −sin.
x(t) and x̂(t) have the same energy. For finite-energy real signals, their inner product is zero.
The ideal Hilbert transformer is non-causal; practical 90° phase-shifting networks approximate it over a band.

blocks.text: The analytic signal, also called the pre-envelope, is x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t). For a real band-pass signal, x<sub>a</sub> has only positive frequencies: its spectrum is 2X(f) for f > 0 and 0 for f < 0. The factor 2 keeps the real part unchanged.

blocks.where: x<sub>a</sub>(t) is the analytic signal in volts; x(t) is the real band-pass signal in volts; x̂(t) is its Hilbert transform in volts; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: The complex envelope removes the carrier: x̃(t) = x<sub>a</sub>(t)e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>. It is low-pass and complex. It is not the analytic signal; x<sub>a</sub> still contains e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>.

blocks.where: x̃(t) is the complex envelope in volts; x<sub>a</sub>(t) is the analytic signal in volts; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz; t is time in seconds.

blocks.text: Canonical representation of a band-pass signal uses the in-phase and quadrature components:
x(t) = Re{x̃(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>} = x<sub>I</sub>(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − x<sub>Q</sub>(t) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)
blocks.where: x<sub>I</sub>(t) = Re{x̃(t)} is the in-phase component in volts; x<sub>Q</sub>(t) = Im{x̃(t)} is the quadrature component in volts; Re{·} means real part; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz; t is time in seconds.

blocks.text: Downconversion multiplies x<sub>a</sub> by e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> and low-pass filters to get x̃. Upconversion takes Re{x̃ e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>} to rebuild x(t). In a receiver, multiply x(t) by 2cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and −2sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), then low-pass filter, to get I and Q.

A band-pass system has a low-pass equivalent. Let h(t) be the real band-pass impulse response. Its complex envelope h̃(t) is defined by h(t) = Re{h̃(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}; that is, h̃(t) is the complex envelope of h(t). The output complex envelope is:

blocks.where: ỹ(t) is the output complex envelope in volts; x̃(t) is the input complex envelope in volts; h̃(t) is the complex envelope of the band-pass impulse response h(t), that is, h(t) = Re{h̃(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}; * is convolution; the 1/2 follows from the analytic-signal convention.

blocks.text: The output is y(t) = Re{ỹ(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>} with ỹ = (1/2) x̃ * h̃. Keep the 1/2 factor consistent; dropping it changes the gain by 6 dB. Some syllabi call the complex envelope the low-pass equivalent. This view reduces simulation and design to low-pass filters and complex arithmetic.

Phase shifting: a 90° phase shifter over the band approximates the Hilbert transformer. In single-sideband (SSB) generation, one path is direct and the other is Hilbert-transformed; adding or subtracting cancels one sideband. See Unit 2, SSB and VSB modulation, for the circuit.

figure.caption: The Hilbert transformer creates the quadrature signal. Adding j x̂ gives the analytic signal, and multiplying by e^(−j2πfc t) leaves the complex envelope 1.732 + j1.000 V. The last block rebuilds the real band-pass signal.

spec.title: Hilbert transform to complex envelope
spec.aria: A block diagram from x(t) through a Hilbert transformer to x̂(t), then to analytic signal, complex envelope, and back to x(t).

examples.question: A band-pass voltage is x(t) = 2 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V with f<sub>c</sub> > 0. Find the Hilbert transform x̂(t), the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub>(t), the complex envelope x̃(t), and the I and Q values at t = 0.
steps: The Hilbert transform of cos is sin for a positive carrier. So x̂(t) = 2 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V.
Form the analytic signal: x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t) = 2[cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) + j sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)] = 2e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)</sup> V.

Convert to rectangular form: 2 cos 30° = 2(√3/2) = 1.732 V; 2 sin 30° = 2(0.5) = 1.000 V. Thus x̃(t) = 1.732 + j1.000 V. The complex envelope is constant for this pure tone, so at t = 0 it has the same value.
I = Re{x̃} = 1.732 V and Q = Im{x̃} = 1.000 V. Check: 1.732 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − 1.000 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) equals 2 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V.
examples.answer: x̂(t) = 2 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°) V; x<sub>a</sub>(t) = 2e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°)</sup> V; x̃(t) = 1.732 + j1.000 V; I = 1.732 V, Q = 1.000 V.
examples.check:
import math
A = 2.0
theta = math.radians(30.0)
I = A * math.cos(theta)
Q = A * math.sin(theta)
print(f'{I:.3f}')
print(f'{Q:.3f}')

traps: The Hilbert transform of cos is sin, not −sin. The −j factor shifts the positive-frequency phasor by −90°, and cos(θ − 90°) = sin θ.
x̃(t) is not the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub>(t). The analytic signal still contains e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>; the complex envelope has the carrier removed.
H(f) = −j sgn(f), not −j for all frequencies. Negative frequencies get +90°, which keeps the time signal real.
In low-pass equivalents, keep the 1/2 factor from the analytic-signal convention. Dropping it changes the gain by 6 dB.

quiz.q: State the frequency response and phase shift of the ideal Hilbert transformer.
quiz.a: H(f) = −j sgn(f). Magnitude is 1; phase is −90° for f > 0 and +90° for f < 0; at f = 0 the response is 0.

quiz.q: Why does x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t) remove negative frequencies?
quiz.a: For f < 0, H(f) = +j, so j·H(f)·X(f) = j(j)X(f) = −X(f); the spectrum is X(f) − X(f) = 0. For f > 0, H(f) = −j, so j·H(f)·X(f) = j(−j)X(f) = +X(f); the spectrum is X(f) + X(f) = 2X(f). Negative frequencies cancel, positive frequencies double.

quiz.q: For x(t) = 4 cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°) V, find x̂(t), x<sub>a</sub>(t), x̃(t) and I/Q.
quiz.a: x̂(t) = 4 sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°) V; x<sub>a</sub>(t) = 4e<sup>j(2πf<sub>c</sub>t − 45°)</sup> V; x̃(t) = 4e<sup>−j45°</sup> = 2.828 − j2.828 V; I = 2.828 V, Q = −2.828 V.

quiz.q: A student says H[cos] = −sin because −j is a −90° shift. Identify the error.
quiz.a: The −90° rotation acts on the positive-frequency phasor e<sup>jθ</sup>. cos(θ − 90°) = sin θ. So H[cos] = sin, not −sin.

quiz.q: Give the canonical I/Q form of a band-pass signal.
quiz.a: x(t) = x<sub>I</sub>(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − x<sub>Q</sub>(t) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), where x<sub>I</sub> and x<sub>Q</sub> are real low-pass components.

quiz.q: Why can a band-pass filter be replaced by a low-pass filter on complex envelopes? Mention the factor.
quiz.a: Analytic signals convolve as y<sub>a</sub> = (1/2)x<sub>a</sub> * h<sub>a</sub>. Pulling out e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> gives ỹ = (1/2)x̃ * h̃. The real part returns the band-pass output; the 1/2 comes from the analytic-signal definition.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined radios digitise I and Q directly after a quadrature downconverter, so later filtering and demodulation run at a low rate. Image rejection and I/Q gain or phase imbalance are practical problems in that chain. Simulation tools use the same complex-envelope view to model a band-pass system as a low-pass equivalent. Search for 'analytic signal', 'IQ data' and 'complex envelope' to go deeper.
